doc.title: Reggie Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, May 22, 2018

title: Time travel to 1959 and musicians' sense of history
summary: Watkins would visit New York in 1959 and thinks musicians then knew they were making history, despite discrimination.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I mentioned earlier, you went into trad jazz clubs and so forth. If you could do time travel would you go back to a certain era to witness particular jazz events?
Hmm that’s a good question. I think I would go ahead and do the 1959 thing you know.
Yeah 1959 was big. I think I would probably do 1959. Just drop me off in New York and just let me — I’ll figure it out you know.
You sometimes wonder — did those musicians have a sense that what they were doing on these particular sessions or playing in these particular venues was historical. © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

Because if you look at some of those old clips of shows where they’re introducing — of course the musicians were celebrated to a certain extent. On the other hand of course horrible discrimination and whatnot was going on in our country. But artistically they were being validated not only by their peers but by the media and by listeners in other countries. And if you were a jazz musician in the fifties and you went to Europe you would feel that sense of appreciation. You know, that maybe you aren’t getting in the United States. But I think a lot of them knew. You know you see — Duke Ellington lived long enough to understand that he was not just a successful band leader and composer/arranger, but also celebrated as a national treasure. I mean a lot of the things that were said about Duke Ellington were said while he was alive. You know, greatest American composer of all time. That kind of stuff. Some of them knew.
